compact_payload.Source/Guideline: Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline
compact_payload.Question: A 62-year-old man has newly diagnosed high-risk localized prostate cancer and asks for focal HIFU instead of surgery or radiation. What counseling best matches guideline-based management?
compact_payload.Option A: Offer focal ablation as standard first-line therapy
compact_payload.Option B: Pair focal ablation with concurrent BCG
compact_payload.Option C: Do not recommend focal or whole-gland ablation outside a trial
compact_payload.Option E: Use surveillance alone because disease is localized
compact_payload.Explanation: Option C is correct. High-risk localized prostate cancer should be managed with definitive local therapy pathways, and focal or whole-gland ablation should not be recommended outside a clinical trial. Option A is incorrect because ablation is not the standard first-line option for high-risk disease. Option B is incorrect because BCG treats bladder cancer, not localized prostate cancer. Option D is incorrect because tissue biomarkers do not replace staging and risk-based treatment selection. Option E is incorrect because surveillance alone undertreats high-risk disease in a fit patient. Teaching point: High-risk prostate cancer is not the setting to convert an unproven focal therapy into standard curative treatment. Source: American Urological Association. Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline.

compact_payload.Source/Guideline: Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline
compact_payload.Question: An 86-year-old man has high-risk localized prostate cancer, obstructive local symptoms, severe frailty, and limited life expectancy. Which plan may be reasonable?
compact_payload.Option A: No symptom-directed cancer treatment can be offered
compact_payload.Option C: Focal ablation as curative standard therapy
compact_payload.Option D: Palliative ADT alone after goals-of-care discussion
compact_payload.Option E: Cystectomy because the symptoms are obstructive
compact_payload.Explanation: Option D is correct. For selected high-risk localized prostate cancer patients with local symptoms and limited life expectancy, palliative ADT alone may be appropriate after shared decision-making. Option A is incorrect because palliation can be appropriate when cure-directed therapy is not. Option B is incorrect because major surgery is not mandatory in a severely frail patient with limited life expectancy. Option C is incorrect because focal ablation is not guideline-standard high-risk treatment. Option E is incorrect because cystectomy is not treatment for localized prostate cancer obstruction. Teaching point: Localized prostate cancer management still accounts for frailty, symptoms, and life expectancy, not risk group alone. Source: American Urological Association. Clinically Localized Prostate Cancer: AUA/ASTRO Guideline.

compact_payload.Source/Guideline: Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline
compact_payload.Question: A 71-year-old woman has a new papillary bladder tumor resected at TURBT. No upper-tract imaging has been performed. What belongs in the initial evaluation?
compact_payload.Option B: No imaging unless flank pain occurs
compact_payload.Option C: Defer upper-tract imaging until risk stratification is complete after pathology returns
compact_payload.Option D: Use cystoscopic surveillance alone without anatomic imaging
compact_payload.Explanation: Option A is correct. Initial evaluation of a patient with bladder cancer includes upper urinary tract imaging to assess for synchronous upper-tract disease and complete staging context. Option B is incorrect because imaging is part of initial evaluation rather than only symptom-triggered. Option C is incorrect because upper-tract imaging should not be deferred until after pathology-based risk stratification; it belongs in the initial evaluation. Option D is incorrect because cystoscopic surveillance alone cannot assess the upper urinary tract. Option E is incorrect because cytology alone cannot replace anatomic upper-tract assessment. Teaching point: Bladder cancer evaluation is not limited to the visible bladder tumor; the upper tracts must be considered at diagnosis. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Treatment of Non-Muscle Invasive Bladder Cancer: AUA/SUO Guideline.

compact_payload.Source/Guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
compact_payload.Question: A 44-year-old man passes his first kidney stone and brings the fragment to clinic. Before deciding whether metabolic prevention is needed, what should be done?
compact_payload.Option A: Discard the stone if symptoms resolved
compact_payload.Option B: Send the stone for composition analysis
compact_payload.Option D: Treat first stones as cystine stones by default
compact_payload.Option E: Use urine dipstick pH as the sole classifier
compact_payload.Explanation: Option B is correct. When a stone is available, stone analysis should be obtained at least once because composition changes prevention counseling and medication choices. Option A is incorrect because symptom resolution does not remove the value of composition data. Option C is incorrect because acetohydroxamic acid is reserved for selected infection-stone situations, not empiric first-stone prevention. Option D is incorrect because cystine stones are uncommon and require confirmation. Option E is incorrect because urine pH alone cannot determine stone composition. Teaching point: Stone analysis is a low-burden step that prevents guessing at the metabolic pathway. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

compact_payload.Source/Guideline: Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline
compact_payload.Question: A 52-year-old woman with recurrent stones transfers care. She has scattered outside reports but no clear current burden. What review should guide prevention planning?
compact_payload.Option B: Use serum creatinine as the stone-burden estimate
compact_payload.Option C: Assume no stones if pain is absent
compact_payload.Option D: Use urine culture colony count as stone size
compact_payload.Option E: Assess or obtain imaging to quantify stone burden
compact_payload.Explanation: Option E is correct. AUA medical management emphasizes reviewing available imaging or obtaining imaging to quantify stone burden, because prevention intensity and follow-up depend on whether stones are present and progressing. Option A is incorrect because waiting for surgery misses the chance to plan prevention and surveillance. Option B is incorrect because kidney function does not measure stone number or size. Option C is incorrect because asymptomatic stones can still be present. Option D is incorrect because culture results do not quantify stone burden. Teaching point: Medical stone prevention starts with knowing both composition and current burden, not symptoms alone. Source: American Urological Association. Medical Management of Kidney Stones: AUA Guideline.

compact_payload.Source/Guideline: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
compact_payload.Question: A 78-year-old woman with severe OAB asks for a chronic urethral Foley solely for incontinence after medications and procedures were intolerable. What counseling is required?
compact_payload.Option A: Recommend catheterization routinely before behavioral therapy
compact_payload.Option B: Use a larger balloon if leakage occurs
compact_payload.Option C: Discuss chronic catheter as a last-resort option with harm counseling
compact_payload.Option D: Promise it prevents urinary tract infection
compact_payload.Option E: Use urethral catheterization to preserve the urethra
compact_payload.Explanation: Option C is correct. Chronic indwelling urethral or suprapubic catheters for OAB should be considered only when other therapies are contraindicated, ineffective, or no longer desired, and only with shared decision-making about harms. Option A is incorrect because catheterization is not routine early OAB therapy. Option B is incorrect because increasing catheter size or balloon volume can worsen urethral injury. Option D is incorrect because chronic catheters increase infectious and other complications. Option E is incorrect because urethral catheters can cause urethral trauma and erosion. Teaching point: A chronic catheter is an incontinence-management fallback, not a benign OAB treatment. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.

compact_payload.Source/Guideline: The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder
compact_payload.Question: A 59-year-old woman with idiopathic OAB wants to choose between behavioral therapy, medication, and PTNS based on goals and adverse effects. How should options be framed?
compact_payload.Option A: Require failure of multiple behavioral therapies before discussing medication
compact_payload.Option B: Use shared decision-making without a rigid step-therapy sequence
compact_payload.Option D: Delay treatment until urodynamics is abnormal
compact_payload.Explanation: Option B is correct. The OAB guideline frames treatment as shared decision-making across therapy categories rather than a mandatory rigid step-therapy ladder. Option A is incorrect because patients do not have to exhaust every behavioral option before medication discussion. Option C is incorrect because invasive therapy is not the default starting point. Option D is incorrect because urodynamic abnormality is not required before treatment in uncomplicated idiopathic OAB. Option E is incorrect because patients may use options from more than one category when appropriate. Teaching point: Modern OAB management is preference-sensitive and category-based, not a forced linear checklist. Source: American Urological Association. The AUA/SUFU Guideline on the Diagnosis and Treatment of Idiopathic Overactive Bladder.

compact_payload.Question: A 46-year-old woman has trace blood on dipstick at a work screening but no microscopic urinalysis yet. What should happen before labeling microhematuria?
compact_payload.Option A: Proceed directly to cystoscopy and CT urography
compact_payload.Option C: Obtain formal microscopic evaluation of the urine
compact_payload.Explanation: Option C is correct. Positive dipstick blood should prompt microscopic urinalysis, and microhematuria should not be defined by dipstick alone. Option A is incorrect because full urologic evaluation depends on confirmed microscopic RBCs and risk stratification. Option B is incorrect because dipstick alone is insufficient. Option D is incorrect because intravesical therapy treats bladder cancer contexts, not an unconfirmed screening dipstick. Option E is incorrect because a positive dipstick merits confirmation rather than dismissal. Teaching point: The first hematuria decision is diagnostic confirmation, then risk-based evaluation. Source: American Urological Association. Microhematuria: AUA/SUFU Guideline.

compact_payload.Source/Guideline: Diagnosis and Management of Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline
compact_payload.Question: A 39-year-old man has pelvic pain for 4 months with dysuria-like flares. Before diagnosing CP/CPPS, which basic evaluation element is expected?
compact_payload.Option B: Prescribe a 4-week fluoroquinolone course before any urine testing
compact_payload.Option C: Skip physical examination if PSA is normal
compact_payload.Option D: Midstream urine culture with assessment for confusable disorders
compact_payload.Option E: Defer confusable disorder exclusion until three treatment courses fail
compact_payload.Explanation: Option D is correct. Initial male chronic pelvic pain evaluation includes history, examination, laboratory assessment such as urinalysis and midstream urine culture, and exclusion of confusable disorders. Option A is incorrect because infection should not be assumed without appropriate testing. Option B is incorrect because empiric fluoroquinolone treatment before urine testing risks unnecessary antibiotics and misses the required baseline evaluation. Option C is incorrect because physical examination remains part of evaluation. Option E is incorrect because confusable disorders should be considered during initial evaluation, not deferred until repeated treatment failures. Teaching point: CP/CPPS is a diagnosis made after structured evaluation, not after reflex labeling of pain as infection. Source: American Urological Association. Diagnosis and Management of Male Chronic Pelvic Pain: AUA Guideline.

compact_payload.Source/Guideline: Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline
compact_payload.Question: A 41-year-old woman with recurrent uncomplicated UTIs wants prophylaxis but strongly prefers to avoid continuous antibiotics. Which option may be offered?
compact_payload.Option B: Daily fluoroquinolone as the default option
compact_payload.Explanation: Option E is correct. Methenamine hippurate may be offered for prophylaxis in women with recurrent uncomplicated UTIs and can serve as an antibiotic-sparing prevention option. Option A is incorrect because routine monthly upper-tract imaging is not part of recurrent uncomplicated UTI prophylaxis. Option B is incorrect because continuous fluoroquinolone prophylaxis is not the default preventive pathway and carries avoidable harms. Option C is incorrect because cystoscopy is not required before each prophylactic dose. Option D is incorrect because asymptomatic bacteriuria should not drive indefinite treatment. Teaching point: Recurrent UTI prevention includes antibiotic-sparing options when they fit patient goals and evidence. Source: American Urological Association. Recurrent Uncomplicated Urinary Tract Infections in Women: AUA/CUA/SUFU Guideline.
